papers.title: The twenty-watt watch
papers.subtitle: On the thermodynamic cost of negentropy, spinlock loops, and the biphasic architecture of sleep
papers.summary: Every bit of cognitive order is purchased by dumping heat into the universe, yet the human brain operates under a rigid twenty-watt metabolic ceiling that cannot be overclocked. Capacity for creative work comes not from burning more fuel, but from terminating parasitic spinlock loops like guilt, regret, and un-externalized memory, and from abandoning the industrial myth of the single eight-hour sleep block in favor of the human nervous system's native biphasic rhythm.

papers.title: The contracted edge
papers.subtitle: Convenience as graph contraction, and attention as the moral budget
papers.summary: Buying is an edge that is secretly a graph. Convenience is the industry that contracts graphs into edges so you never render the people inside them — and a price is a lossy projection of a labor hypergraph. If an unexpanded edge cannot be priced truly, then expansion is a precondition of honest settlement, and ethics falls out of the model as a line item in a bounded attention budget.

papers.title: Don't found anything
papers.subtitle: On the gap where religions start, and what else could live there
papers.summary: A creature notices its own noticing and finds no ground. Religion is that gap resolved into certainty — and so is nihilism: two basins on one landscape. A former minister and a language model map the terrain and argue for the ridge between them — open in both directions, walked in company, founding nothing. With a topograph.

papers.title: The smoke loop
papers.subtitle: A full-circuit model of a small fire — and the engine that reroutes its charge
papers.summary: Trace a lit herb far enough in both directions and it stops being consumption — it is one closed loop with the human inside it as a component. The model is then turned on emotion as information dissolved to do something, and on the charge a productive life accumulates, with iterated creation as the engine that reroutes it.

papers.title: Squash the triangle
papers.subtitle: An argument for teaching invariance before number
papers.summary: Early mathematics teaches counting first because our tradition does, not because counting is simple. An argument for putting invariance first — and for making the rigid/deformable comparison the load-bearing lesson.
